how do I install system updates
answer:
On InterGenOS you keep everything current with **pkm**, the package manager. Two steps:

```
pkm sync       # refresh the package index from the mirror
pkm upgrade    # install newer versions of everything installed
```

`pkm sync` pulls the latest signed package index, then `pkm upgrade` rebuilds-or-fetches and installs the newer versions. You can run `pkm upgrade` on its own, but syncing first makes sure you're seeing everything that's available.

answer:
Install software with **pkm**:

```
pkm install <name>
```

For example `pkm install htop`. pkm handles everything in the InterGenOS repositories, so it's the one command you need. If you're not sure of the exact package name, search first with `pkm search <term>`.

Proprietary apps (Chrome, VS Code, etc.) aren't in the repos — they're installed through their download-helpers, e.g. `pkm install vscode` pulls the vendor installer rather than a repackaged binary.

answer:
Remove software with **pkm**:

```
pkm remove <name>
```

For example `pkm remove htop`. (`pkm uninstall` works too — it's an alias.) pkm won't let you remove a package that others still depend on without telling you; configuration files you've edited under `/etc` are preserved on removal.

answer:
Search the repositories with **pkm**:

For example `pkm search editor` lists matching packages with a short description. Once you know the name, `pkm info <name>` shows the full details, and `pkm install <name>` installs it.

answer:
List and inspect installed packages with **pkm**:

```
pkm list              # everything installed
pkm info <name>       # full details for one package (version, files, deps)
pkm files <name>      # the files a package owns
```

To check whether something specific is installed, `pkm info <name>` succeeds if it's present and tells you it's not otherwise.

how do I detect modified package files
answer:
Verify installed packages against their recorded SHA-256 hashes with **pkm**:

```
pkm verify           # check every installed package
pkm verify <name>    # check just one
```

This re-hashes the files each package owns and reports any that differ from what was installed — a fast integrity check for tampering or corruption. Configuration files you've intentionally edited under `/etc` are expected to differ and are reported as such, not as damage.

triggers: explain how package management works
how does package management work
how do packages work on InterGenOS
what is pkm
how does pkm work
tell me about package management
answer:
InterGenOS manages all software with one tool, **pkm** — the single front door:

```
pkm sync             # refresh the signed package index from the mirror
pkm upgrade          # update everything installed
pkm install <name>   # add a package
pkm remove <name>    # remove one
pkm search <term>    # find a package
pkm list             # what's installed
pkm verify           # check installed files against their recorded hashes
```

Every package is fetched against a signed, pinned index and verified by SHA-256, so what you install is exactly what was published — integrity is checked, not assumed. `pkm sync` then `pkm upgrade` is the routine to stay current.

triggers: how do I install software on linux
answer:
InterGenOS installs software with **pkm**. Sync the index, then install by name:
```
sudo pkm update          # refresh the package index (verifies its signature)
sudo pkm install <name>  # e.g. sudo pkm install neovim
```
pkm pulls in dependencies automatically and verifies each archive's SHA-256 against the
signed index before extracting. Search first if you're unsure of the name: `pkm search <term>`.

triggers: how do I install a .deb file
answer:
You can't — InterGenOS is a from-source distro with its own format (`.igos.tar.gz`), not
Debian's, so `.deb` packages are not compatible and there is no `dpkg`/`apt`. Install the
InterGenOS build of what you want instead:
```
pkm search <name>
sudo pkm install <name>
```
If it's a proprietary app (Chrome, VS Code, Spotify, Discord), pkm ships a download-helper —
just `sudo pkm install chrome` (etc.). If nothing matches, the app isn't packaged yet.

triggers: how do I uninstall a program
answer:

pkm cleanly removes the package and offers to drop orphaned dependencies no longer needed by
anything else. To sweep all orphaned dependency-installed packages at once: `sudo pkm autoremove`.

triggers: how do I install google chrome
answer:
Chrome is proprietary, so InterGenOS ships a **download-helper** rather than bundling it. Same
command as any package:
```
sudo pkm install chrome
```
pkm shows a consent pause, then runs Google's "I ACCEPT" EULA and downloads the real Chrome.
(An open alternative that's built from source and needs no EULA: `sudo pkm install firefox`.)

triggers: how do I install vlc
answer:
InterGenOS doesn't ship VLC. The included, from-source media player is **mpv** (plus the
Celluloid GTK front-end and Rhythmbox for music):
```
sudo pkm install mpv          # command-line + desktop player
sudo pkm install celluloid    # GNOME/GTK front-end for mpv
```
mpv plays essentially everything VLC does. If you specifically need VLC, it isn't packaged yet.

triggers: what's the difference between snap, flatpak and apt
answer:
None of those exist on InterGenOS. There's no apt, no snap, and no flatpak — the one package
manager is **pkm**, which installs from-source InterGenOS builds verified against a signed
index. There are no sandboxed universal bundles; everything is a first-class native package.
Proprietary apps (Chrome, VS Code, Spotify, Discord) come via `pkm install <app>` download-
helpers. Everyday commands: `sudo pkm update`, `pkm search <term>`, `sudo pkm install <name>`,
`sudo pkm upgrade --all`.

triggers: where's the app store
answer:
InterGenOS has no graphical app store; software is managed with the **pkm** command line. To find and install things:
```
pkm search <term>            # browse the index
pkm info <name>              # details
sudo pkm install <name>      # install
```
`pkm list available` shows everything in the synced index.

triggers: how do I upgrade to the latest version
answer:
If you mean upgrading your installed packages to their latest versions:
```
sudo pkm update
sudo pkm upgrade --all
```
InterGenOS is a rolling-package system — there's no separate "release upgrade" step; keeping
packages current via `pkm upgrade --all` keeps you on the latest. (The OS-image/kernel is
handled through pkm too; `linux-kernel` upgrades require the explicit `--allow-kernel-replace`
flag as a safety gate.)

triggers: how do I update just one program
answer:
Name the package explicitly:
```
sudo pkm update            # refresh the index first
sudo pkm upgrade <name>    # upgrade only that package
```
Naming packages bypasses the `--all` requirement. If it's held, `pkm unhold <name>` first.

triggers: do I need to reboot after updating
answer:
Usually no. pkm never auto-restarts services during an upgrade (you control when your machine
takes downtime). After an upgrade, restart affected services yourself:
```
pkm restart-services --list     # shows what wants a restart vs a reboot vs nothing
sudo pkm restart-services --all # restart the running services pkm packages own
```
A reboot is only needed for a **kernel** upgrade (`linux-kernel`); `restart-services --list`
flags that as `reboot`.
